term_glossary.tooltip: High Bandwidth Flash: a NAND-based, non-coherent, read-optimized memory tier placed close to an accelerator.
High Bandwidth Memory: stacked DRAM used as high-bandwidth working memory near accelerators.
A generic processing unit such as a GPU, TPU, CPU, or specialized accelerator.
Key-value tensors retained from earlier tokens and layers to accelerate autoregressive decoding.
The bottom HBF die that manages host traffic, UCIe, the NAND stack, and test/debug paths.
The NAND die stack above the HBF Base die.
Through-silicon via: a vertical electrical connection through stacked dies.
Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express: an open, on-package die-to-die interconnect standard.
Advanced eXtensible Interface: the AMBA transaction protocol carried over the HBF UCIe streaming link.
Optional, per-channel volatile memory for high-priority temporary data at latency on the order of an L3 cache.
Mixture of Experts: a model architecture that activates selected expert subnetworks for each input or token.

slides.title: AI Growth Turns Data Movement into the Bottleneck
slides.subtitle: Model weights and KV cache grow alongside compute demand.

bullets.text: Accelerators can wait when memory cannot supply data at the required rate.
Larger models, longer contexts, and more users increase weight and KV-cache traffic.
Adding GPUs partly to obtain more attached HBM can waste compute and power.
HBF adds high-capacity NAND close to the accelerator with wide, parallel read access.

figure.alt: Animation showing compute demand, model weights, and KV cache outgrowing a two-tier HBM and SSD path before HBF opens a high-capacity path near the xPU.
figure.caption: The memory wall becomes a data-movement problem as model state grows faster than the local memory tier.

slides.title: HBF Fills the Space Between HBM and SSDs
slides.subtitle: The tiers cooperate; HBF does not universally replace either neighbor.

bullets.text: Ultra-fast stacked DRAM for the most latency-sensitive accelerator working set.
NAND-based, non-coherent, read-optimized capacity close to the xPU.
Durable, high-capacity storage that remains the source of truth for permanent data.
Place hot working data in HBM, large read-dominant AI data in HBF, and durable copies on SSDs.

figure.alt: Three-tier AI memory hierarchy with HBM nearest compute, HBF as a high-capacity on-package tier, and SSD as persistent storage.
figure.caption: HBF introduces a managed tier between working memory and persistent storage.

slides.title: From Industry Proposal to Open OCP Architecture
slides.subtitle: Shared boundaries let processor, memory, package, and software ecosystems develop together.

bullets.text: Sandisk and SK hynix began HBF standardization work.
A dedicated effort formed under the OCP Storage Project in early 2026.
Version 0.7.0 defines interface, protocol, electrical, packaging, reliability, software, security, and application boundaries.
The first open architecture specification launched alongside the industry event.

slides.title: The Gap HBF Is Designed to Fill
items: AI inference makes data movement a primary system constraint.
HBF augments HBM and SSDs with a new NAND-based tier near the xPU.
The OCP specification defines open integration boundaries rather than one complete vendor product.
A 512 GiB density calculation and three bandwidth grades frame version 0.7.0.
Sixteen-channel parallelism is the foundation for aggregate performance.

slides.subtitle: Answer both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry.

questions.prompt: Which description best matches HBF's intended system role?

choices.text: A NAND-based, high-capacity tier near the xPU that augments HBM and SSD storage
A direct replacement for all HBM in every workload
choices.feedback_incorrect: HBF targets HBM-class aggregate read bandwidth with more capacity, but HBM remains the ultra-fast working-memory tier.

choices.text: A persistent SSD interface moved onto the processor package
choices.feedback_incorrect: HBF is NAND-based, but it uses a distinct non-coherent memory-centric UCIe/AXI architecture rather than an SSD block interface.

choices.text: A coherent cache that automatically manages every AI data structure
choices.feedback_incorrect: The specification describes HBF as non-coherent and assigns important placement and lifecycle responsibilities to host software.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. HBF adds a high-capacity, high-bandwidth tier between HBM and persistent SSD storage.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the three-tier model: HBM handles the hottest working set, HBF adds large near-xPU capacity, and SSDs preserve durable data.

questions.prompt: Which characteristics belong to the OCP HBF architecture? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Sixteen independent host channels
Read-optimized NAND-based capacity
Non-coherent operation near the xPU
Unlimited write endurance
Permanent-storage replacement for SSDs

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. HBF combines a near-xPU, non-coherent NAND tier with sixteen parallel host channels.
questions.feedback_incorrect: HBF is read-optimized and endurance-limited. The specification still recommends persistent storage such as SSDs for permanent data.

slides.title: A Base Die Coordinates a 16-Die NAND Stack
slides.subtitle: Control logic and dense media are optimized separately, then joined vertically.

bullets.text: Manages host traffic, UCIe, NAND communication, and test/debug paths.
Sixteen NAND dies provide the stack's capacity.
Vertical connections route signals between the Base die and NAND stack.
The complete stack sits close to the host compute die over a short electrical path.

figure.alt: Exploded HBF stack showing the Base die, sixteen NAND Core dies, TSV connections, and the nearby xPU.
figure.caption: The Base die translates host transactions into managed operations across the NAND Core die stack.

slides.title: Sixteen Independent UCIe Channels Build Bandwidth
slides.subtitle: Each channel is a self-contained x64 advanced-package link.

bullets.text: An x64 channel reaches this raw bandwidth at 32 GT/s.
Mission data stays separate from bring-up, training, configuration, and management.
Format 6 uses a latency-optimized 256-byte flit with optional bytes.
Channels are independently clocked and need not be synchronous with one another.

figure.alt: One UCIe x64 HBF channel expanded into mainband, sideband, protocol, adapter, and physical layers, repeated across sixteen channels.
figure.caption: A repeated short-reach link creates aggregate bandwidth without one monolithic bus.

slides.title: AXI Transactions Are Shaped Around Flash Geometry
slides.subtitle: A familiar transaction model carries explicit alignment and page rules.

bullets.text: 64 B through 4 KiB, in 64 B multiples, aligned and contained within one 4 KiB page.
A complete 4 KiB burst begins on a 4 KiB-aligned address.
One, two, or four interfaces per UCIe channel support workload-selected interleaving.
Ready/valid and credits move requests and responses while permitting out-of-order reads.

figure.alt: AXI read and write examples aligned to 64-byte segments and a 4 KiB NAND page, including a prohibited cross-page read.
figure.caption: AXI lowers protocol overhead without hiding NAND-page constraints.

slides.title: Parallelism Is Designed into Every Layer
items: The Base die coordinates host traffic and a stack of sixteen NAND Core dies.
Sixteen independent UCIe channels create the aggregate host path.
AXI over UCIe keeps protocol overhead low while preserving flash geometry.
Reads remain inside 4 KiB page boundaries; writes assemble aligned 4 KiB units.
Global-to-local address interleaving determines how much parallel bandwidth software can use.

slides.title: Check Your Parallel-Bandwidth Model
slides.subtitle: Answer both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry.

questions.prompt: At 32 GT/s, what raw bandwidth does one x64 HBF UCIe host channel support?

choices.text: 256 GB/s
32 GB/s
choices.feedback_incorrect: 32 GT/s is the line rate. The x64 data width produces 256 GB/s for one channel.
3.072 TB/s is the maximum user-bandwidth grade for the complete sixteen-channel device, not one channel.
4,096 GB/s is the raw total across all sixteen channels at the maximum grade.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Eight bytes per transfer times 32 GT/s gives 256 GB/s per channel.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Separate the per-channel calculation from the sixteen-channel aggregate.

questions.prompt: Which host behaviors support correct, high-throughput HBF access? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Keep reads within a 4 KiB NAND-page boundary
Use aligned 4 KiB writes
Interleave suitable data across AXI paths and host channels
Assume one channel can access another channel's NAND resources
Concentrate every hot region in one channel

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Alignment, complete logical units, and broad channel use activate the architecture safely.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Requests remain channel-local. A hot region concentrated in one channel cannot use the full device bandwidth.

slides.title: Software Sees Sixteen Independent Linear Spaces
slides.subtitle: HBF and HBM are managed separately, and channel reads do not share one global order.

bullets.text: HBM and HBF use distinct regions because capacity and access behavior differ.
Each UCIe channel exposes its own continuous logical address range.
Maximum performance comes from issuing work to as many channels as possible.
Per-channel SRAM can hold high-priority temporary data but does not survive a power cycle.

figure.alt: Separate HBM and HBF address regions, with the HBF region divided into sixteen channel-local linear spaces and optional scratchpad SRAM.
figure.caption: The global map is a software policy; each HBF channel remains an independent local resource.

slides.title: Parallel Reads Are Easy; Writes Need Structure
slides.subtitle: Read broadly, write complete pages, and manage wear explicitly.

bullets.text: Channels operate independently and may complete out of order.
Pages inside one NAND block progress in order even while different blocks run in parallel.
HBF does not automatically move active data between physical locations.
Base-die or host-controlled wear leveling redirects channel-local addresses to new physical locations.

figure.alt: Comparison of parallel HBF reads, sequential writes within NAND blocks, and host-controlled hot-zone to cold-zone remapping.
figure.caption: HBF exposes flash lifecycle behavior instead of hiding it behind an SSD controller model.

slides.title: Reliability Is a Shared Contract with the Host
slides.subtitle: The Base die reports state; host software turns that state into policy and recovery.

cards.title: Endurance
cards.body: Monitor maximum and average program/erase counts; lifecycle is workload- and product-dependent.

cards.title: Refresh
cards.body: Schedule product-defined refresh, typically every 24–48 hours, and respond to read-disturb risk.

cards.title: Thermals
cards.body: Operate across normal, light-throttling, severe-throttling, and shutdown states from 0°C to 105°C.

cards.title: Errors
cards.body: Retry, refresh, replay, wait, or retire capacity according to the reported condition.

cards.title: Security
cards.body: Power-on erase and sanitize are optional, product-specific controls rather than universal inline protection.

cards.title: Durable copy
cards.body: Use persistent storage such as SSDs for permanent data and recovery sources.

slides.title: Place Model Weights and KV Cache Deliberately
slides.subtitle: Different read/write patterns deserve different channel and zone policies.

bullets.text: Read-dominant data favors full-channel interleaving for repeated token-generation access.
Prefill creates it; decode repeatedly reads and extends it as sequences grow.
Equal channel groups simplify host-driven wear leveling between weights and KV cache.
Size channel groups to a known model to maximize remaining capacity.

figure.alt: HBF channels partitioned into model-weight and KV-cache regions using uniform and non-uniform allocation strategies.
figure.caption: The host chooses a balance among bandwidth, endurance, and capacity utilization.

slides.title: HBF Performance Depends on Placement
items: HBF and HBM are managed as separate tiers with sixteen HBF local spaces.
Reads favor broad parallelism; writes retain NAND sequencing and page rules.
Host software participates in wear, refresh, recovery, thermals, and security policy.
Interleaving maximizes bandwidth; dedicated channels improve isolation and allocation control.
Weights and KV cache need distinct placement policies because their write behavior differs.

slides.title: Check Your HBF Serving Strategy
slides.subtitle: Answer both questions once to continue. Correctness is not required, and you can retry.

questions.prompt: Which placement strategy best maximizes HBF bandwidth for one large model?

choices.text: Stripe the model across all suitable host channels and read them in parallel
Place the complete model in one channel
choices.feedback_incorrect: One channel limits the model to that channel's bandwidth. Full interleaving activates the aggregate device.

choices.text: Rewrite every weight page during each generated token
choices.feedback_incorrect: Weights are read-dominant after placement. Rewriting them per token would add unnecessary NAND wear and traffic.

choices.text: Rely on HBF garbage collection to redistribute hot data
choices.feedback_incorrect: HBF does not provide conventional garbage collection or automatic active-data movement.

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. Full-channel interleaving gives one large model access to the aggregate read path.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Review the relationship between channel-local placement and aggregate bandwidth.

questions.prompt: Which responsibilities remain with host software in an HBF system? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Schedule refresh and respond to read-disturb risk
Monitor wear and apply the selected zone-remapping policy
Handle retry, replay, wait, and capacity-retirement actions
Choose channel placement for weights and KV cache
Assume every product implements the same optional security and scratchpad features

questions.feedback_correct: Correct. HBF is a hardware-software contract, and the host owns important lifecycle and placement policy.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Optional features vary by product. The host must discover capabilities and still manage refresh, wear, recovery, and placement.
